teamStories.title: All eyes on not only Fernando Mendoza’s growth, but Klint Kubiak too
teamStories.summary: From the quarterback adjusting to blitzes and the coach and play caller involving others, there’s plenty to do
teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images In terms of accountability, the Las Vegas Raiders have that locked down at the all-important head coach and quarterback spot with Klint Kubiak and Fernando Mendoza, respectively. After the team’s 21-13 defeat at hands of the visiting Seattle Seahawks this past Sunday — dropping the team to 4-6 overall — both Kubiak and Mendoza went up the podium to shoulder the blame. “I thought overall when we lost Brock (Bowers), you definitely saw a big change in production,” Kubiak said after the game when asked about the simple gameplan and stagnant offense against Seattle. “So I look at myself; I have to do a much better job of moving the ball, getting and spreading the ball around.” So I got us in the wrong check, and then they sacked me, and that’s why a lot of the sacks today, if not all of them, were on me, not on the offensive line,” Mendoza said in particular of Seahawks nickel corner Devon Witherspoon sacking him twice off slot blitzes. “I thought they played great and displayed great leadership today, and I need to be better, especially with those DB blitzes.” Watching the Raiders franchise quarterback getting absolutely walloped by ‘Spoon and other Seahawks defenders was certainly not ideal. But welcoming the brunt of the blame and pointing the finger at themselves, one could even label the Silver & Black’s promising head coach and quarterback combo the “I-Twins” as their quick to pin the blame on themselves and note they must improve for the overall good of the team. And that’s an endearing trait for two key figures in the organization that are rookies in their respective roles. Fernando Mendoza: Before this sack (13 dropbacks): +0.47 EPA per dropback (would rank 1st in the NFL) 10/12, 83 yards 0 sacks After (25 dropbacks): -0.47 EPA per dropback (would be last) 7/17, 60 yards (with 38 yards coming on a Jeanty checkdown) 5 sacks pic.twitter.com/oCr4rp87PT — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) November 17, 2026 While we won’t know what’s said behind closed doors at Raiders headquarters, the practice field, or in the locker room game days — there have been few instances where I was privy too and within earshot of tirades in post game locker room access — we were given a glimpse of Kubiak’s fury when the CBS broadcast captured the moment he was talking to his offensive line on the sidelines . So while it’s admirable Kubiak stands in front of media row and says it’s “my fault”, it’s good to see that Kubiak doesn’t absolve his team of their own responsibilities. But the following day, during his media session on Monday, Kubiak ensured it’s also a “we” thing. “I think overall, as an offensive line, there’s a solid first half of run game production followed by a very poor half of protection, and that’s not all on them,” the Raiders rookie head coach said. “That’s on getting open, that’s on getting rid of the ball, that’s on play calls. It’s a team thing. So, we win together and we lose together.” Kubiak was also quick to note that his side of the ball — the offense — didn’t play enough complementary football when Rob Leonard’s defense helped maintain a 10-3 advantage against Seattle — precarious as that lead may be. Sure, losing Bowers — an elite pass catcher who Kubiak deploys as equal parts wide receiver and tight end — scuttled things and plans went awry against the Seahawks. And once Mike Macdonald recognized that Mendoza can not only throw dimes but also fire lasers on the run and take off to gain yards with his legs, the Seahawks’ defensive mastermind dialed up man concepts with blitzes. And the results speak for themselves. Mendoza said getting punched in the face gives him the opportunity to watch his mistakes and grow from them. Kubiak, too. And it’s integral that duo take these tough growing pains and apply the lessons going forward. “I love Klint.” “This is well coached football team.” “This team has a future.” Mike MacDonald on seeing his former offensive Cordinator Klint Kubiak today. #RaiderNation #Seahawks pic.twitter.com/np9gKp0Fis — Armani Lingo (@armani_lingo8) November 16, 2026 Because what Seattle put on tape defensively against the rookie quarterback will become a regular occurrence — until — Mendoza shows consistently that he can identify the pressure, adjust protection, let the other 10 players on offense what’s up, and burn the defense when they bring the pain. The good old Uno reverse card, if you will. That noted, the 6-foot-5, 225-pound No. 1 overall pick from the 2026 NFL Draft showed he is NFL ready by not only standing in the pocket and progressing through his read and firing, scrambling for positive yards when he needed to, but also hanging onto the football when he got waylaid. Even when Mendoza was rocked, he didn’t suddenly see ghosts and get happy feet. He got up, went back to the huddle, barked out the play and went about his business. The mental and physical toughness are ideal. The footwork, the arm, the legs, and the mind all show Mendoza can play at the pro level and if protected, can succeed. And the miscues from the 23-year-old Indiana product are fixable. Now, it’s about Kubiak, offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko, quarterback coach Mike Sullivan, offensive line boss Rick Dennison to speak to their players and get the offense aligned. Protect the franchise and good things happen. And franchise, take care of yourself and don’t take those hits that can cause fright — for the fanbase and yourself. Kubiak provided insights on what he wants to see going forward. Fernando Mendoza on his first start: "It's good to get punched in the face because now it's a great opportunity to grow and learn… and to really unveil all the deficiencies that I have in my game as a future hopeful leader of this offense." pic.twitter.com/LT8Mf0yjwG — Arye Pulli (@AryePulliNFL) November 16, 2026 “Well, remain a passer. Number one, keep your eyes downfield. Remain a passer like he did to Jack Bech on that left sideline, like he did to Ian (Thomas) early in the game, getting through his progression,” the head coach and play caller said. “Remain a passer, and then obviously protect yourself when you start to run down the field.” “Yeah, it wasn’t up to our standard for quarterback hits and sacks,” Kubiak said about the six sacks and 12 quarterback hits Mendoza absorbed. “That’s an entire offensive stat. It’s getting open fast, that’s protecting better, and that’s him getting rid of the ball. There’s three things there.” While it’d be grand if Kubiak, Janocko, Dennison and Co. can get the run blocking to be on par with the pass protection to give their young quarterback a ground game he can rely upon, that’s been a longstanding issue when heady veteran Kirk Cousins was under center. But there’s signs that Mendoza has the ability to become the leader — not hopeful leader as he said above — of the Raiders offense. And boy, that’ll be a sight to behold, when it does happen.

teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders received good news ahead of their Week 11 matchup against the Denver Broncos . ESPN’s Ryan McFadden posted a video of tight end Brock Bowers in full pads and participating in warmups ahead of Thursday’s practice, noting that Bowers is returning to the field. #Raiders TE Brock Bowers (ankle) returns to practice on Thursday. pic.twitter.com/p467LGyArL — Ryan McFadden (@ryanmcfadden_) November 19, 2026 The Raiders’ leading receiver exited last week’s game against the Seattle Seahawks at halftime and missed Wednesday’s session with ankle and quadricep injuries. This was a step in the right direction for Bowers’ availability on Sunday against the Broncos, as the Raiders listed him as limited on the injury report (h/t The Athletic’s Sam Warren ). Also, Las Vegas’ offense really needs its top target. The ‘tight end’ has racked up 50 catches for 676 yards and six touchdowns in eight games this season, leading the Silver and Black in all three categories despite missing the first two contests with a knee injury. According to Sumer Sports , the team’s passing game averages 0.105 EPA per pass and has a 49.0 percent success rate with Bowers on the field this year. Without him, those numbers dip to 0.005 EPA per pass and 43.4 percent. Factor in that rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza will be making his second career start against a Denver defense that ranks ninth in points per game allowed ( 20.7 ), and it’s even more important that Bowers suits up on Sunday. Additionally, Warren noted that guard Trey Zuhn III (illness), defensive tackle Tonka Hemingway (stinger) and defensive tackle Foley Fatukasi (toe) weren’t spotted during the media viewing period of Thursday’s practice. Zuhn wasn’t listed on Wednesday’s report, while Hemingway was a non-participant and Fatukasi was limited on Wednesday. Neither of the three linemen participated in Thursday’s session. If Zuhn can’t go, second-year guard Caleb Rogers is likely the next man up. Rogers replaced Zuhn when the latter left the 49ers game with a concussion a couple of weeks ago. Hemingway’s and Fatukasi’s absence would really test the Raiders’ defensive tackle depth, a position that’s been an issue all season. That would likely mean more reps for Adam Butler, Tim Keenan III, Thomas Booker IV and JJ Pegues. Warren also reported that the Raiders brought in kickers Lucas Havrisik, Younghoe Koo and John Parker Romo for a workout, as Matt Gay is dealing with a hip injury and sat out of practice. Tight end Ian Thomas added an ankle injury to Thursday’s report after missing Wednesday with a calf injury, though Thomas was upgraded to limited on Thursday. As for the Broncos, they managed to get healthier for the second practice of the week. The only changes from yesterday’s injury report were cornerback Kris Abrams-Draine (ankle), defensive tackle Zach Allen (rest) and wide receiver Courtland Sutton (rest) going from limited to full participants. Brock Bowers was a limited participant in his return to practice today. Matt Gay did not participate in practice despite being present, hence the kicker tryouts today. teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 11 is the start of a stretch where the Las Vegas Raiders will face a divisional opponent in three of their next four games, beginning and ending that stretch with the Denver Broncos . It will also mark rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza’s second career start, and the Raiders will need to be on point in the trenches to pull off the 9.5-point upset on the road . That leads us into this week’s key matchups for Las Vegas. Raiders’ OTs vs. Broncos’ Edge Rushers Mendoza had a shaky starting debut last week against the Seattle Seahawks, completing 17 of 29 pass attempts (58.6 percent) for 143 yards and no touchdowns . The biggest reason for that is that he, understandably, struggled to handle Mike Macdonald’s exotic pressure looks and ended up taking six sacks. The good news for the Raiders is there probably isn’t a more difficult defensive scheme for a rookie quarterback to handle than the Seahawks’. The bad news is the Broncos also have an elite pass-rush, and defensive coordinator Vance Joseph isn’t shy about bringing the heat. According to Sumer Sports , Denver ranks fourth in pressure rate (41.6 percent) and 11th in blitz rate (33.7 percent). For comparison, the Seahawks are eighth in pressure (40.9 percent) and 28th in blitz (23.0 percent), as Macdonald uses more simulated pressures rather than pure blitzes. But more than anything, what really makes Denver’s pass-rush so effective is its edge rushers: Nik Bonitto and Jonathon Cooper. Bonitto has made Pro Bowls in back-to-back seasons by racking up 27.5 sacks over the last two years. Through nine games in 2026, he’s posted 4.5 sacks and has 30 pressures, according to Pro Football Focus . The latter ranks 19th among edges despite recording the third-fewest pass-rush snaps (228) of anyone in the Top 20. Additionally, his 19.4 percent pass-rush win rate is sixth-best and 90.5 pass-rush grade is third-best. Of the fifth-year pro’s 387 defensive snaps, 340 have come as a right outside linebacker , setting up for a long battle between him and Raiders’ left tackle Kolton Miller. While Miller has a track record of being a good pass-protector, he’s been regressing this season by giving up 32 pressures in 10 games. For comparison, the 31-year-old surrendered 38 pressures in 2024, which is the most recent season where he played in all 17 games. So, Vegas will need its left tackle to turn back the clock on Sunday. On the other side of the line, off-field issues led to Cooper spending the first six games of the campaign on the Commissioner’s Exempt List. As a result, he’s only participated in three contests this year and has underwhelming numbers with 0.5 sacks and 10 pressures. However, he has a strong track record with 27 sacks from 2023 to 2025, and finished last year tied for 25th among edge rushers with 51 pressures during the regular season. Meanwhile, Las Vegas’ right tackle, DJ Glaze, is having a career year. After giving up 99 pressures on 1,217 opportunities (about a 12.3-to-one ratio) in his first two seasons, he’s yielded just 15 pressures on 379 opportunities (about a 25.3-to-one ratio). In other words, the third-year pro is getting beaten half as frequently as he used to. Long story short, both of the Raiders’ offensive tackles are capable of keeping Bonitto and Cooper away from Mendoza. But the Broncos’ pair of edge rushers are also more than capable of winning against Miller and Glaze, setting up for an intriguing battle in the trenches. Burford/Zuhn vs. Allen (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images" data-portal-copyright="Getty Images" /> Continuing with the theme above, Zach Allen has established himself as one of the best interior pass-rushers in the NFL. He’s racked up 25 sacks in 3.5 seasons with the Broncos and is coming off a first-team All-Pro campaign, where he accumulated seven sacks and led defensive tackles with 73 pressures during the regular season. Through nine games in 2026, Allen has picked up right where he left off, registering 4.5 sacks and topping the charts for his position with 38 pressures . Part of what makes him difficult to contain is that he plays on both sides of the line, with 238 of 442 snaps coming on the left this year and 175 on the right, per PFF . That allows Joseph to move the disruptive defensive tackle around and take advantage of an opponent’s weakest guard. So, both Spencer Burford and Trey Zuhn III have to be on point to keep Allen in check. That could be an issue for Burford, who enters the weekend tied for the third-most pressures ( 23 ) among guards this season. To be fair, his 379 opportunities are tied for the seventh-most at the position, so volume does play a factor in that number. However, a bottom-20 96.6 PFF pass-blocking efficiency rating isn’t much better. Meanwhile, Zuhn has only made three starts at guard and thus has only yielded five pressures on 85 opportunities. A sample size that small means the jury is still out on the rookie, and a 97.2 efficiency rating isn’t something to write home about. To paint a picture of how much the position has been a sore spot for Vegas: Zuhn’s efficiency rating is the highest of the team’s guards this season, and it ranks tied for 37th across the league . That sets up a big mismatch that Klint Kubiak will have to account for to keep Mendoza upright. Of course, the interior line having its best game of the year wouldn’t hurt, either. Crosby/Koonce vs. Bolles/McGlinchey Bo Nix has been one of the worst quarterbacks under pressure this season. According to PFF , his 10 ‘turnover-worthy plays’ under pressure are tied for the fourth-most among QBs with at least 182 total dropbacks. Also, his 8.6 percent TWP rate is the third-highest, and his 26.5 passing grade is the third-worst. However, Nix has only been under pressure on 34.9 percent of his dropbacks, which is the 12th-best rate at the position. That’s, at least partially, a testament to the two bookends the Broncos have at offensive tackle: Garrett Bolles and Mike McGlinchey. Bolles has a history of being a stingy pass-protector, and that hasn’t changed in 2026. He’s yielded just five pressures on 307 opportunities, which is the fewest of any offensive tackle with at least 239 snaps in pass protection, per PFF . Unsurprisingly, the two-time All-Pro’s 99.2 efficiency rating also tops the charts at his position this year. Meanwhile, McGlinchey doesn’t have quite as impressive a resume as Bolles does, but the right tackle is putting together a strong performance this fall. On 307 opportunities, he’s yielded just 19 pressures and has a 96.7 PFF efficiency rating. The former is one shy of the top 25 for the position, and the latter sits exactly at 25th. Seeing as Foley Fatukasi leads the Raiders defensive tackles who have at least 100 pass rush snaps this season with a 6.9 percent pass-rush win rate , which ranks 69th among NFL defensive tackles, the Silver and Black are going to have to get pressure around the edge to get to Nix. Despite facing a high rate of double teams and opponents constantly sliding their pass protection to him, Crosby still has five sacks and ranks tied for fourth among edge rushers with 46 pressures this season. His pass-rush win rate has dipped since the beginning of the year but still sits at 16.2 percent and is tied for 18th at his position. The five-time Pro Bowler isn’t the reason Vegas has a below-average pressure rate (37.4 percent), sitting at 18th in the league, according to Sumer . In fact, he’s the biggest reason the figure is even that high. But Crosby needs more help from his running mate, Malcolm Koonce, who started the campaign hot but has cooled off recently. In Weeks 1-5, the sixth-year veteran was tied for 21st among edges with 16 pressures and sixth with a 19.4 percent win rate . In the five games since then, he’s tied for 64th in pressures (eight) and tied for 65th in win rate (10.0 percent) . Clearly, the Raiders need the complementary rusher who got off to a strong start to show up on Sunday and not the guy they’ve had over the last month. Otherwise, expect Nix to have all day to throw while Crosby continues to fight through chip blocks and double teams.

teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) The Las Vegas Raiders head on the road to Empower Field to take on the division-leading Denver Broncos in a renewal of an AFC West rivalry. A win against the Broncos will go a long way to instilling confidence in rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza and the defense. Furthermore, the Raiders contest against the Cleveland Browns has been flexed to Sunday Night Football and could be a game with potential playoff implications. Can the Raiders find a way to beat the Broncos? Division games are a funny thing; typically, you can throw out records and standings. Both teams are configured to beat each other, if not play to an absolute standstill. This game is no different; while the records are nearly opposite- Broncos (7-2), Raiders (4-6) their strengths cancel each other out and the weaknesses will be the difference makers. Broncos Defense by the numbers The Broncos’ defense hasn’t been what it used to be, ranking 26 th in total defense. The defense is ranked near the bottom third of the league in every category except points (9 th ) and takeaways (12 th ). Their rushing defense is ranked 23th, allowing 1119 yards in total rush yards, 26 th in yards per carry (4.5), but T-4 th in rushing touchdowns with six. Surprisingly, the Broncos have surrendered one less, (9) 20+ yard carry than the Raiders defense (10) and one more 40+ yard carry (2). Here’s where it gets rougher for the Raiders and young signal caller Mendoza: the Broncos are 4 th -lowest in completion percentage (60.2), T-5 th lowest in yards per attempt (6.5). Additionally, being T-6 th in multiple categories: in sacks (26) and interceptions (8). Ranking 8 th in quarterback rating (83.4), with the only blemish being T-6 th most passing touchdowns (14) A bunch of fancy statistical numbers to say that you can, in fact, move the ball up and down the field on this Broncos defense, unlike in years past. The flip side to that is that it’s still just as hard to score on them. Potential Raiders plan of attack Can the Raiders devise a way to beat the Broncos? Yes, they can. Possibly being without, or having a limited, Brock Bowers emphasizes a change in tactics for Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak. In a pinch, Michael Mayer has been magnificent when factored into the game plan; Tre Tucker has game-breaking speed when assigned a featured role as well. Ian Thomas has contributed in the passing game; the Raiders could also throw a friendly face in with Mendoza and play wide receiver, Malik Benson. Short yardage/ red zone conversions have been catastrophic for the Raiders in 2026; the run game hasn’t been much better. In the first half of the game against the Seattle Seahawks, they found a way to generate some success. They will need to refine what was working and continue to apply it for a complete game to bring balance to the offense. The running backs, both Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington Jr are going to need to put on some bifocals to see the holes to run through. Until the run-blocking execution improves, both backs are going to need to be able to make at least one defender miss. Moreover, both should employ a tactic like Fred Biletnikoff’s stick-em and coat their jerseys in Pam cooking spray or some sort of slick material. Making it hard to grab hold of them and easier for them to break away from would be tacklers. Al Davis had two rules: #1 cheating is encouraged, #2 See rule #1. Need a better gameplan Kubiak must have a game plan that isn’t solely reliant on #89, more so one using him as a potential decoy until he can get into the red zone or critical situations. The need to spread the football around to keep the Broncos’ defense off balance will aid his young quarterback tremendously. He will also need to account for only being able to get roughly two quarters’ worth of success maximum out of every plan he rolls out. His opening scripts are magnificent, but when the defense makes adjustments, the struggles will begin. A razzle-dazzle play, or something creatively complex and unique to call, that hasn’t been put on tape in 10 weeks will help. Three or four such plays would be ideal, whether he already has them in the playbook or not. Perhaps tweak his wide receiver deployment and utilize Jack Bech out wide; move either Jalen Nailor or Tre Tucker into the slot. Maximize the downfield blocking ability of Bech and get looser coverage on one of the other two speedier receivers. Scheme blitz beaters in the play calls, the NFL is a copycat league, a smart defensive coordinator would try to replicate what the Seahawks did last Sunday. Shotgun draws, delayed zone runs and more running back screens can help slow down the rush. Kubiak is a passing game genius; the offensive line may be more of an obstacle, but it can be overcome.
